top_choice_rationale: P002 (Rubinstein and Wolinsky) has the clearest conceptual content and the cleanest attribution on the slate. Rubinstein's alternating-offers model is the originating result, and Wolinsky's market-bargaining extension is distinct. The model has about forty years of validated use in price formation, wage setting and search models, and earlier game-theory prizes covered equilibrium, information and mechanism design rather than the bargaining process itself. Its direct empirical bite is indirect and Binmore and Stahl complicate the lineage, so I treat these as real discounts, but a two-name citation is defensible. P005 (Melitz and Helpman) is a strong mechanism, but credit for Bernard, Eaton, Jensen and Kortum cannot be honoured and the welfare estimates depend on specification. P001 (Autor, Dorn, Hanson) is a serious option on a narrow China-shock citation, though the magnitudes and shift-share identification remain contested. P003 is still young and relies on restricted data. P004 has a mixed empirical record. A prize is preferred to no award.
recusal_note: No recusal-level connection is apparent from the profile. None of my co-authors (Asplund, Steen, Ulsaker, Gronqvist, Wilander, Syverson, Goldstein) is credited on any proposal. I co-authored a 2026 paper with chair John Hassler and former chair Tore Ellingsen, who are not credited on any slate proposal. P005 is adjacent to my IO and trade field, which I disclose as familiarity rather than merit. My spouse's public political role (Magdalena Andersson) is noted as a public fact only and has no apparent bearing on any proposal.
